one_liner: Header-only open-addressing C++ hash table family; emhash7 beats std::unordered_map on insert/find/erase/iterate at 10M elements.
what_it_does: emhash is a header-only family of open-addressing hash tables (emhash5/6/7/8 plus emilib1-4) that replace std::unordered_map/std::unordered_set. The API is a near drop-in: operator[], find, insert, emplace, erase, reserve, and range-for match std::unordered_map, but reference/iterator stability and node handles are not provided. Each numbered variant tunes a different tradeoff (small-table SBO, erase speed, high load factor, dense iteration) rather than offering one universal implementation.
how_it_is_fast: emhash7 stores key-value pairs inline in one contiguous array plus a separate bitmask for fast empty-slot scanning, and repairs the bucket chain on erase instead of leaving tombstones, so mixed insert/erase workloads don't degrade even at load factor 0.999. Iteration is a straight scan of that array, which is why it beats std::unordered_map's pointer-chasing linked-node layout by roughly 85x on the 10M-element iterate benchmark. The emilib variants instead use Swiss-table-style SIMD group probing with a 1-byte H2 tag per bucket to filter most candidates before a full key comparison.
when_to_use: Mixed insert/find/erase workloads on integer or POD keys where throughput close to hand-tuned open addressing matters (emhash7)
Need a load factor above 0.9 (up to 0.999) without the clustering/degradation open addressing usually shows at that density
Iteration-heavy hot paths over the whole map/set (emhash7/emhash8), since the flat array scan beats std::unordered_map's node chasing by an order of magnitude
Want a header-only, dependency-free drop-in (copy one .hpp) rather than adding a build dependency
Input keys are trusted/internal, not adversarially chosen
when_not_to_use: Code holds long-lived references or pointers into the map across inserts — open addressing invalidates them on rehash; std::unordered_map does not

Keys come from untrusted/adversarial input: emhash7/8 don't cap probe-sequence length by default, which SECURITY.md flags as a hash-flooding DoS risk unless you enable EMH_SAFE_HASH or switch to an emilib EMH_SAFE_PSL variant
Multiple threads write concurrently without your own locking — emhash provides no internal synchronization

You want independently reproduced numbers rather than the vendor's own benchmark (emhash's table is self-measured on one Windows/GCC config, not verified here against Ankerl 2022 or Allan 2024 methodology)
Very large value types where rehash-driven moves are costly and you haven't wrapped them in unique_ptr

integration.dependencies: none (wyhash is bundled in config.hpp; pass -DEMH_NO_BUILTIN_WYHASH to supply your own)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (some examples use C++20); GCC, Clang, or MSVC
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux, macOS; x86-64 and ARM64 (Apple M1/M2). emhash5-8 are scalar (no SIMD requirement); emilib variants add SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512 group probing where available
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe. Concurrent writes require an external mutex; concurrent read-only access (find/contains/count) with no active writer is safe (per docs/usage_notes.md)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — operator[], find, insert, emplace, erase, reserve, begin/end, load_factor, etc. match std::unordered_map's signatures, but there is no reference/iterator stability guarantee, no node handle, and bucket()/bucket_size() require the EMH_STATIS build flag

gotchas: emhash7/8 do not cap probe-sequence length by default; SECURITY.md calls this a hash-flooding DoS risk on untrusted keys. Mitigate with EMH_SAFE_HASH (~10% overhead) or an emilib EMH_SAFE_PSL variant
Any insert that triggers a rehash invalidates all existing references and iterators, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability
Erasing inside a plain range-for is undefined behavior; use the iterator-returning erase(it) or erase_if() instead

Some thirdparty/emilib variants (e.g. emilib2ss) can degrade into a full table scan under an all-keys-collide attack; the maintained include/emilib/emihmap2.hpp (emilib2::HashMap) is not the affected fork, but pick emilib2o/emilib2s for untrusted input regardless
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick emhash over rigtorp::HashMap, ska::flat_hash_map, or tsl::robin_map/hopscotch_map when you need a load factor up to 0.999 without tombstone-driven degradation on mixed insert/erase workloads, or want a matched family (emhash6/7/8) tuned per access pattern instead of one fixed design. Pick a sibling instead when you want a single implementation whose speedup was measured by an independent, cross-library suite (e.g. Ankerl 2022) rather than the vendor's own benchmark.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 7 5800H / Windows 10, GCC 11.3 (-O3 -march=native -std=c++17) build, emhash7 beat std::unordered_map (libstdc++) at 10M integer-key elements: insert ~4.5x (66.0 vs 295), find-hit ~2x (16.9 vs 33.0), find-miss ~2.9x (18.1 vs 52.0), erase ~14x (20.4 vs 293), and iterate ~85x (0.74 vs 62.6). These are the project's own docs/performance.md numbers, reproducible via bench/ebench but not independently re-run for this entry.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-05, v1.1.0) and MIT-licensed; header-only, so a single .hpp such as hash_table7.hpp can be vendored with no external dependency.
